strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters should be selected for downstream adaptability rather than only pretraining validation loss. The main empirical finding that larger pretraining weight decay can improve fine-tuned performance, even when it worsens pretraining loss, is practically relevant for LLM training pipelines.

The experimental scope is substantial: two architecture families, several model sizes up to 4B, compute-optimal and overtrained regimes, six downstream CoT fine-tuning tasks, and multiple evaluation metrics including greedy, pass@16, majority, reward-model selection, and reward score.
The paper is clearly written and well organized. It provides useful appendices with model architectures, data sizes, pretraining/fine-tuning hyperparameters, and per-task evaluation plots.

The mechanistic probes are a useful addition. The analyses of linear separability, attention pseudo-rank, and train-validation gap do not prove causality, but they help characterize how weight decay changes pretrained models beyond scalar validation loss.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence appears to rely on single training runs per weight-decay setting, with no random seeds, confidence intervals, or variance estimates. Given the often small downstream differences and noisy fine-tuning/evaluation pipelines, this weakens the strength of the claims about optimal weight decay.

The definition of plasticity is operationalized as final fine-tuned task performance. This conflates adaptability with other factors such as initial capability, representation quality, fine-tuning hyperparameter compatibility, and benchmark-specific effects. Direct measures such as learning curves, sample efficiency, adaptation speed, or controlled equal-loss comparisons would make the plasticity claim stronger.

The weight-decay sweeps are uneven. Llama-2-4B has only two values, OLMo-2-140x has only three, and the overtrained setup also differs in learning-rate schedule. This limits confidence in claims about optimal values and scaling with training duration.

The mechanistic section is mostly correlational. Linear probing accuracy and attention pseudo-rank may be consequences of the same training differences rather than mechanisms causing improved fine-tuning. The overfitting analysis is shown mainly for OLMo-2-1B-20x, so its generality is unclear.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many hyperparameters and dataset details, but does not clearly state whether code, checkpoints, exact data preprocessing, evaluation scripts, prompts, and reward-model scoring code will be released. Reproducing the full study would require very large compute.

The limitations and ethics treatment is thin. The discussion mentions scale/training-duration limits and trade-offs, but there is little explicit discussion of benchmark contamination, reward-model bias in ORM/RM metrics, downstream safety/alignment implications, or environmental/compute cost.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters should be selected for downstream adaptability rather than only pretraining validation loss. This is a useful framing for modern LLM training pipelines.

The experimental effort is nontrivial, spanning two model families, several model sizes up to 4B, two token-per-parameter regimes, and six downstream fine-tuning tasks with multiple evaluation metrics.
The main empirical observation is interesting: in several settings, larger pretraining weight decay appears to improve post-SFT task performance even when it does not minimize pretraining loss.
The appendices provide many relevant implementation details, including model configurations, training data sizes, optimizer settings, SFT hyperparameters, datasets, and weight decay grids.
weaknesses: The central claim that weight decay improves 'plasticity' is not fully supported. The measurement is downstream performance after SFT, which conflates plasticity with base-model quality, representation quality, task alignment, and fine-tuning hyperparameter interactions. The paper does not directly measure learning speed, adaptation curves, amount of new information acquired, or controlled forgetting/adaptation behavior.

The evidence is much weaker than the broad claims suggest. Several key settings use very sparse sweeps: Llama-2-4B has only two weight decay values and OLMo-2-1B-140x has only three. These are then used to support claims about optimal weight decay and training-regime trends, including extrapolations beyond the observed range.

There is no apparent replication across random seeds, no confidence intervals, and little statistical testing. Because both pretraining and fine-tuning are noisy, single-run curves and averaged plots are insufficient to establish robust optima or reliable improvements, especially when some differences appear modest.

The fine-tuning protocol is not sufficiently controlled to isolate pretraining weight decay. The same SFT hyperparameters are used across pretrained models, but models trained with different weight decay may require different fine-tuning learning rates, schedules, or epochs. Without SFT hyperparameter sweeps or adaptation curves, the reported gains may reflect interaction with a fixed SFT recipe rather than intrinsic plasticity.

The mechanistic section is mostly correlational and speculative. Linear probing on SST and AG News, attention pseudo-rank measurements, and a train-validation gap for only OLMo-2-1B-20x do not establish that these mechanisms cause improved downstream adaptation. Some mechanistic evidence is narrow, and the relationship between reduced attention rank and better plasticity is asserted more than demonstrated.

The paper overstates its conclusions. Phrases such as one of the first rigorous empirical demonstrations and claims of optimal weight decay larger than 0.1 are not justified by the limited grids, missing uncertainty estimates, and lack of large-scale or heavily overtrained validation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables. The manuscript does not clearly provide code, checkpoints, exact evaluation prompts/parsers, random seeds, numerical result tables, or enough detail to reproduce all reward-model and sampling evaluations. Many results are only visible as dense plots.

The evaluation design raises concerns. Several downstream tasks are CoT-style and some test choices involve datasets related to fine-tuning sources; possible contamination, overlap, and answer-extraction reliability are not discussed in enough depth. ORM-based solution-quality evaluation also relies on an external reward model without sufficient validation or bias analysis.

Limitations are acknowledged in discussion, but not treated with enough force. The paper notes uncertainty for larger and more overtrained models, yet still presents broad recommendations for pretraining practice. Ethical considerations are essentially absent, despite medical/biomedical evaluation tasks and reward-model-based assessment.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored question: pretraining hyperparameters are usually selected by validation loss, but the work asks whether they also affect later fine-tuning plasticity. This is a useful framing for modern LLM training pipelines.

The empirical effort is substantial. The authors sweep pretraining weight decay across two model families, several scales up to 4B parameters, 20 TPP and 140 TPP regimes, and six downstream CoT fine-tuning tasks with multiple correctness and quality metrics.

The main result is practically significant: larger pretraining weight decay can yield worse pretraining loss but better downstream fine-tuned performance, especially shown by the OLMo-2-1B-140x comparison where weight decay 0.3/1.0 has higher pretraining loss than 0.1 but better downstream results.

The paper goes beyond headline benchmark results by probing possible mechanisms: linear separability of representations, pseudo-rank of attention matrices, and train-validation gaps. These analyses are not fully causal, but they make the contribution more informative than a pure hyperparameter sweep.

Presentation is generally clear. The experimental setup, datasets, weight decay values, model configurations, and fine-tuning hyperparameters are described in enough detail to understand the study design, and the authors appropriately acknowledge that optimal weight decay depends on objective, model size, and training duration.
weaknesses: The central interpretation equates downstream fine-tuning performance with plasticity, but this is only a proxy. Better downstream accuracy may reflect differences in pretrained representations or task-relevant capability rather than a cleaner notion of capacity to adapt. Additional measures such as learning curves during fine-tuning, adaptation speed, or controlled reinitialization/feature-freezing experiments would strengthen the claim.

Several important comparisons are sparse. The 4B Llama setting has only two weight decay values, and the 140 TPP OLMo setting has only three. This makes the claimed optima and trends less secure for the most practically relevant larger or overtrained regimes.

The experiments appear to use single training runs per configuration, with no clear reporting of variance across pretraining seeds or fine-tuning seeds. Given the relatively small downstream differences in some plots, uncertainty estimates or repeated fine-tuning runs would be important for soundness.

Some mechanistic analyses are correlational and occasionally over-interpreted. Linear probe accuracy and attention pseudo-rank correlate with downstream performance, but the paper does not establish that these mechanisms cause improved plasticity. The attention-rank story is also complicated by schedule differences noted for OLMo 140 TPP.

The study fixes many interacting hyperparameters, especially fine-tuning learning rate, epoch count, and batch size. It remains unclear whether high-weight-decay pretrained models are intrinsically more plastic or simply better matched to the chosen fine-tuning recipe.

Reproducibility is partial. The manuscript gives many implementation details and cites repositories used, but I did not see a clear artifact statement committing to release all checkpoints, code, data preprocessing scripts, prompts, evaluation scripts, and reward-model scoring details. Full reproduction would be expensive and difficult without these artifacts.

Limitations are discussed honestly, especially regarding very large and heavily overtrained models, but the ethics/societal impact discussion is minimal. Since the work involves medical QA and reward-model evaluation, a brief discussion of evaluation limitations and misuse risks would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexamined question: how pretraining hyperparameters affect post-training adaptability rather than only pretraining validation loss. The core message that weight decay can improve downstream plasticity despite not always optimizing pretraining loss is useful for LLM training practice.

The experimental scope is a major strength. The authors vary weight decay across Llama-2 and OLMo-2 style models, model sizes up to 4B, 20 TPP and 140 TPP regimes, and evaluate on CoT reasoning, language/commonsense tasks, and safety alignment. The additional sweeps over pretraining learning rate and fine-tuning hyperparameters make the empirical pattern more convincing.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It separates pretraining-loss optima from downstream-performance optima, gives detailed hyperparameter tables, and includes a candid limitations section noting correlational mechanisms, limited scale, and small sample size for some model groups.

The mechanistic analyses are thoughtful. Linear probing, attention pseudo-rank, and train-validation gap analyses do not prove causality, but they provide plausible explanations and connect the empirical findings to prior work on representations, low-rank regularization, and plasticity.
weaknesses: The main empirical claims rely largely on single pretraining runs per weight-decay value, with no reported random seeds, variance estimates, or statistical uncertainty. Because downstream differences can be modest and LLM fine-tuning/evaluation is noisy, the absence of error bars or repeat runs weakens confidence in claims about optimal values and monotonic trends.

The strongest practical conclusion, that the plasticity-optimal pretraining weight decay is larger than the default 0.1, is still limited in scope. The largest model is 4B, only one overtrained regime is studied, and the OLMo 140 TPP setup differs in schedule from the 20 TPP setup. The paper acknowledges this, but it limits how confidently the recommendation transfers to modern frontier-scale or heavily overtrained models.

Plasticity is operationalized as final downstream performance after SFT. This is reasonable but conflates adaptability with other factors such as retained pretrained capability, representation quality, optimization compatibility with the chosen SFT recipe, and task-specific benchmark effects. More direct measurements of learning speed, sample efficiency, parameter movement, or controlled adaptation would sharpen the central interpretation.

The mechanistic section is explicitly correlational. Claims that lower-rank attention, linearly separable representations, or reduced overfitting explain improved plasticity remain hypotheses; the paper does not include interventions that change these properties independently of weight decay.

Some evaluations have limited evidential weight. The safety alignment study uses 100 harmful prompts and a reward model as judge, and the language/commonsense results are mostly relegated to appendix figures. The presentation would be stronger with aggregate tables, uncertainty, and clearer effect sizes rather than many dense plots.

Reproducibility is partial. The paper gives extensive hyperparameters, datasets, and compute descriptions, and the first page appears to advertise models/code, but the extracted manuscript does not expose concrete repository or artifact links. Full reproduction also requires substantial compute, so releasing checkpoints and exact evaluation scripts is important.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexamined issue: pretraining hyperparameters can affect downstream adaptability, not only pretraining validation loss. This is a useful framing for modern pretrain-then-finetune pipelines.

The experimental scope is broader than many hyperparameter papers: two model families, several sizes up to 4B, 20 TPP and 140 TPP regimes, multiple downstream task families, and additional sweeps over pretraining and fine-tuning hyperparameters.

The main empirical pattern is interesting: in several settings, larger pretraining weight decay improves downstream fine-tuned performance even when it is not optimal for pretraining validation loss. The overtrained OLMo-2 case is a particularly useful example of this tradeoff.

The paper is generally clearly written, with explicit training details, datasets, and weight-decay values. The limitations section is honest about correlational mechanisms, limited scale, and small sample sizes for some model groups.
weaknesses: The central claim is framed as improved 'plasticity', but the measurement is essentially final downstream performance after supervised fine-tuning. This conflates plasticity with better pretrained representations, better initial task ability, different memorization/generalization properties, or easier optimization under the chosen SFT recipe. The paper needs stronger evidence such as adaptation learning curves, pre-finetuning baselines, training-loss reduction rates on new data, matched initial downstream performance, or explicit measures of parameter/representation change during adaptation.

The empirical evidence appears to rely mostly on single pretraining runs per weight-decay setting, with no random seeds or uncertainty estimates. Given that many reported differences are modest and the sample size per model group is as low as 3 or 4 for the most expensive settings, it is hard to distinguish robust effects from run-to-run variation.

Several conclusions are overgeneralized. The title and findings imply that weight decay improves language-model plasticity broadly, but the largest-scale evidence is limited, the 140 TPP result has only four weight-decay values and a different learning-rate schedule, and all models are at or below 4B/1.5B class rather than contemporary frontier scales.

The mechanistic section is suggestive but not decisive. Linear probe accuracy, attention pseudo-rank, and train-validation gap are correlated with weight decay, but the paper does not establish that these mechanisms cause the downstream gains. Some discussion acknowledges this, yet the main text still presents them as explanatory evidence more strongly than warranted.

The hyperparameter sweeps are incomplete relative to the claim. Fine-tuning hyperparameter robustness is tested mainly on OLMo-2-1B-20x and only two datasets for the large SFT sweep; pretraining learning-rate sweeps are also confined to one model setup. This leaves open whether the reported optimum is an artifact of the selected LR/batch/epoch recipe.

The downstream evaluation has reproducibility and reliability gaps. The paper gives many implementation details, but does not provide enough information about released checkpoints/code, evaluation prompts, exact decoding/evaluator settings, data cleaning scripts, or statistical testing. Reward-model-based metrics and the 100-prompt safety evaluation are especially fragile without calibration or human validation.

Ethics and impact discussion is minimal despite experiments on safety alignment and harmfulness. The statement that no societal consequences need highlighting is too cursory for a paper that proposes changing pretraining practices and evaluates safety behavior.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexamined issue: pretraining hyperparameters should be judged not only by base-model validation loss but also by downstream adaptability after further training. This is a useful framing for current LLM development practice.

The empirical evidence is broad and unusually expensive for a hyperparameter study: Llama-2 and OLMo-2 families, sizes up to 4B, both 20 TPP and 140 TPP regimes, CoT reasoning, language/commonsense benchmarks, and a safety-alignment setting.

The central result is well supported: larger pretraining weight decay often improves fine-tuned downstream performance, and the weight decay minimizing pretraining loss can differ from the weight decay maximizing downstream performance. The OLMo-2-1B-140x case is especially compelling because worse pretraining validation loss coincides with better downstream performance.

The authors include useful robustness checks over pretraining learning rate and fine-tuning weight decay, learning rate, and batch size, which reduces the concern that the result is an artifact of a single fine-tuning recipe.

The mechanistic analyses are informative: linear probing, attention pseudo-rank, and train-validation gaps provide plausible explanatory evidence and connect the empirical finding to existing work on plasticity, low-rank attention, and regularization.

Presentation is clear overall. The paper states the research question explicitly, separates pretraining-loss and downstream-performance objectives cleanly, and includes detailed appendices with model configurations, datasets, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The mechanistic claims remain correlational. The paper is appropriately honest about this, but the evidence does not establish that linear separability, lower attention rank, or reduced overfitting cause the improved plasticity.

Some model groups have very few pretraining variants, especially Llama-2-4B-20x and OLMo-2-1B-140x. This limits confidence about the exact optimal weight decay and makes some correlations unstable, even though the qualitative trend is consistent.

The study is still limited to moderate-scale models by frontier standards. The practical recommendation may change for larger models, heavier overtraining, different data mixtures, RLHF/RL post-training, or multimodal models.

The evaluation mostly treats plasticity as final downstream performance after SFT. This is reasonable and useful, but it conflates ease of adaptation with other factors such as representation quality, retained pretraining knowledge, and fine-tuning optimization dynamics.

There is limited reporting of repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Given the cost this is understandable, but it makes it harder to separate small but consistent gains from training/evaluation noise in some plots.

The impact statement is generic. Since the paper includes safety fine-tuning and recommends hyperparameter choices that affect model adaptability, a more concrete discussion of misuse, safety-alignment trade-offs, and deployment implications would strengthen the ethics treatment.
